children.name: Project Description
children.reason:
Evaluation of the README file:

project_purpose:
Score (avg): 5.0
[QWEN] Question evaluated: Does the README describe the project's purpose and why it is useful? Yes, very thoroughly. The opening paragraph states that "CIB seven is a flexible framework for workflow and process automation" whose core is "a native BPMN 2.0 process engine that runs inside the Java Virtual Machine," and immediately explains its utility: it "can be embedded inside any Java application and any Runtime Container," "integrates with Java EE 6," and "is a perfect match for the Spring Framework," with optional tools for "human workflow management, operations and monitoring." The "Components" section concretizes the value by listing the Engine, REST API, Spring/CDI integration, Camunda Modeler, Cockpit, Admin, and Tasklist, and the "A Framework" section explicitly states the project's value proposition and differentiator: "In contrast to other vendor BPM platforms, CIB seven strives to be highly integrable and embeddable. We seek to deliver a great experience to developers that want to use BPM technology in their projects." Purpose and usefulness are both clearly and comprehensively communicated.

setup_instructions:
Score (avg): 2.0
[QWEN] Question evaluated: Does the README describe the setup instructions? Only minimally. The README contains no inline setup instructions whatsoever: there are no prerequisites, no installation or build commands, no version requirements (e.g., Java/Maven versions), and no quick-start example. What it does provide is a "Getting Started: https://docs.cibseven.org/get-started/" link in the main link list, a "manual-latest" badge linking to the external documentation site, and a "Tests" section stating "To run the tests in this repository, please see our testing tips and tricks (TESTING.md)." In other words, all actual setup, build, and run procedures are delegated to external documentation, and a user reading only the README cannot set up the project. The presence of a prominent Getting Started link shows the information is discoverable, but the README itself does not describe setup instructions, so the criterion is only weakly met.

info_project_status:
Score (avg): 2.0
[QWEN] Question evaluated: Does the README describe the project's status (active development, no longer maintained, etc.)? No explicit statement of the project's status appears anywhere in the README: there is no wording such as "actively developed," "in maintenance mode," "no longer maintained," and no information about release cadence or maintenance policy. There are only implicit signals of ongoing activity: the "manual-latest" badge pointing to current documentation, a "Discussions" badge, a link to the Issue Tracker, and a "Contributing" section inviting new code contributions. These clues suggest the project is alive and maintained, but the README never actually describes the project's status, so the criterion is not explicitly satisfied.

info_maintainer:
Score (avg): 2.0
[QWEN] Question evaluated: Does the README describe who maintains and contributes to the project? Only partially and indirectly. The "Contributing" section describes how to contribute ("Please see our contribution guidelines (CONTRIBUTING.md) for how to raise issues and how to contribute code to our project"), and the "And there's more..." section notes that "Community Extensions" are "provided and maintained by our great open source community," with a "Discussions" forum linked for the community. However, the README never names the maintainers or the maintaining organization or team: no maintainer names, no organization/team ownership statement, and no link to a maintainers page or core team. It explains the contribution process but does not describe who actually maintains the project, so the criterion is only weakly addressed.

children.name: Project Structure
children.reason:
Project structure evaluation:

directory_organization:
Score (avg): 4.0
[QWEN] This is a large Java/Maven multi-module monorepo, and it follows the standard Maven directory conventions almost uniformly across all ~100+ modules: each module contains a pom.xml with src/main/java, src/test/java, src/main/resources, and src/test/resources (e.g., engine/, spin/core/, connect/http-client/, model-api/bpmn-model/). Stack-appropriate variant directories are also used correctly: src/main/webapp for WAR modules (webapps/assembly/src/main/webapp, distro/tomcat/webapp/src/main/webapp), src/main/rar for the ESB RAR (javaee/jobexecutor-rar/src/main/rar/META-INF), src/it for integration tests (clients/java/client/src/it), src/main/openapi with schema.json for OpenAPI generation (engine-rest/engine-rest-openapi/), and src/main/less or public/ under the JavaScript frontend (webapps/frontend/). Cross-cutting tooling is sensibly placed: .ci/ for Jenkins pipelines (with config/, daily/, main-trigger/, sidetrack/, scripts/alignment/), .github/ for GitHub workflows and issue templates, settings/ for IDE configuration (eclipse/, intellij-idea/, maven/), qa/ for quality assurance, and root-level docs (README.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, SECURITY.md, TESTING.md). It is not a 5 only because of a handful of deviations from the stack conventions: there is no central docs/ directory (documentation is README.md files scattered per module, plus engine-rest/docs/ which is actually a build tooling directory with package.json and build.js rather than user documentation), distro/cibseven-welcome places WEB-INF/glassfish-web.xml and assets/ directly at the module root instead of under a src/ tree, distro/sql-script uses a non-standard src/main/javadoc/ directory to hold a README.txt, qa/tomcat10-runtime keeps assembly.xml at the top of src/, and javaee/jobexecutor-ra holds META-INF/MANIFEST.MF at the module root outside src/. These are minor, mostly legacy-driven oddities in an otherwise exemplary Maven layout.

naming_conventions:
Score (avg): 4.0
[QWEN] Naming is highly consistent and matches ecosystem conventions across the vast majority of the repository. All top-level and nested module directories use lowercase kebab-case that mirrors Maven artifactId conventions: engine-rest-openapi-generator, spring-boot-starter/starter-webapp-core, identity-ldap, test-db-instance-migration/test-fixture-11, feel-scala, tomcat10-runtime, resources-tomcat10/resources-tomcat11, distro/cibseven-welcome. Configuration and CI files follow the same style: .github/workflows/*.yml (add-issue-to-project.yml, java-dependency-check.yml, scorecards.yml), .ci/scripts/alignment/check-spring-alignment.sh and alignment-lib.sh, kebab-case test resources (logback-test.xml, camunda.ldap.pages.cfg.xml, jboss-deployment-structure.xml, arquillian.xml). Java package roots are consistently renamed to the project name (org/cibseven, visible in engine/src/main/java/org/cibseven/, freemarker-template-engine, juel, qa/test-old-engine/config/org/cibseven/bpm), and shell/batch scripts come in consistent .sh/.bat pairs (start-cibseven.sh/start-cibseven.bat, run.sh/run.bat). The score is not 5 because of a visible inconsistency localized to the legacy JavaScript frontend in webapps/frontend: file names within camunda-commons-ui/lib mix camelCase (HttpClient.js, RequestLogger.js, escape.js, fixDate.js, moduleLoader.js) with kebab-case (cam-local-configuration.js, change-dmn-namespace.js, tests-module.js, create-cam-api-mock.js), and there is even a typo'd name (canocialAppName.js). Test directories are also inconsistent there: camunda-bpm-sdk-js/test/ and camunda-commons-ui/test/ use singular "test" while ui/admin/tests/, ui/cockpit/tests/, ui/tasklist/tests/, ui/welcome/tests/ use plural "tests". Additionally, distro/run alongside distro/run4 is an ad-hoc version-suffixed naming that is hard to interpret. Outside the JS area, naming discipline is essentially uniform, so the overall level is good rather than poor.

separation_of_concerns:
Score (avg): 4.0
[QWEN] Different concerns are placed in clearly delineated, purpose-specific areas. Production source, test source, and resources are separated per the Maven standard in every module (e.g., engine/src/main vs engine/src/test, spin/core/src/main/resources/script vs spin/core/src/test). Testing concerns are further tiered: unit tests live in src/test, integration tests are centralized in the top-level qa/ tree (integration-tests-engine with per-runtime source sets like java-tomcat/java-wildfly-servlet and resources-tomcat/resources-wildfly, integration-tests-webapps, large-data-tests, performance-tests-engine with its own docs/ and perf-test-config.properties, test-db-instance-migration, test-db-rolling-update), and reusable test infrastructure is isolated in test-utils/ (archunit, assert, junit5-extension, junit5-extension-dmn, testcontainers). CI/CD tooling is separated into .ci/ (Jenkins) and .github/ (workflows, issue templates, helpers), while developer tooling configuration sits in settings/ (eclipse, intellij-idea, maven). Dependency governance is split out into bom/ (camunda-bom, camunda-only-bom) and internal-dependencies/, and packaging/distribution concerns are confined to distro/ with per-runtime sub-projects (jboss, tomcat, wildfly, run, run4, sql-script, webjar, license, license-book). Examples are isolated in examples/invoice, and the frontend JavaScript is separated from the Java backend under webapps/frontend with its own package.json, webpack configs, and lint configurations. It does not reach 5 because a few concerns are co-located or duplicated: QA is nested inside some modules (spring-boot-starter/starter-qa, quarkus-extension/engine/qa, distro/run/qa) even though a top-level qa/ exists, creating two competing QA homes; distro/run and distro/run4 form near-duplicate distribution trees (both contain modules/ with ai-agent, example, http-client, oauth2, rest, soap-http-client, webapps), overlapping concerns across versions; and distro/cibseven-welcome mixes static web assets (assets/fonts, assets/img) directly into a Maven module without a src/ boundary.

modularity:
Score (avg): 4.0
[QWEN] The project demonstrates an excellent logical decomposition into independently buildable modules, each with its own pom.xml, mapped to clear domains: the core engine (engine/), decision modeling split into engine-dmn/{bom, engine, feel-api, feel-juel, feel-scala}, REST layering (engine-rest/{engine-rest, engine-rest-openapi, engine-rest-openapi-generator, assembly, docs}), framework integrations as sibling modules (engine-cdi, engine-spring, quarkus-extension/{deployment, runtime, qa}, spring-boot-starter/{starter, starter-client, starter-rest, starter-security, starter-test, starter-webapp, starter-webapp-core}, plus a parallel spring-boot-4-starter), extension points (engine-plugins/{connect-plugin, identity-ldap, identity-scim, spin-plugin}), the connect client family (connect/{core, http-client, soap-http-client, ai-agent, connectors-all, bom}), data-format modules (spin/{core, dataformat-json-jackson, dataformat-xml-dom, dataformat-all}), model APIs per specification (model-api/{xml-model, bpmn-model, dmn-model, cmmn-model}), shared libraries (commons/{logging, typed-values, utils, testing, bom}), distribution per target runtime (distro/{tomcat, jboss, wildfly, run, run4, webjar, sql-script, license-book}), plus cross-cutting modules (clients/java, javaee/{ejb-client, ejb-service, jobexecutor-ra, jobexecutor-rar}, juel, freemarker-template-engine, database, examples, qa, test-utils). Dependency governance is modularized through a parent POM in parent/, the root pom.xml, internal-dependencies/, and multiple BOMs (bom/, engine-dmn/bom, connect/bom, spin/bom, commons/bom), which is a textbook approach for a build of this size. This is held back from a 5 by two version-parallel duplications that weaken the decomposition: distro/run and distro/run4 are duplicated module trees differing mainly by version (run4's modules/ mirror run's modules/ but contain only pom.xml shells), and spring-boot-starter versus spring-boot-4-starter exist side by side, the latter appearing mostly as pom-only placeholders with an awkwardly nested starter-client/spring-boot/ subdirectory. These suggest that version variants were handled by duplication rather than parameterization, a moderate modularity flaw in an otherwise very well-structured module graph.

children.name: Security Policy
children.reason:
Evaluation of the SECURITY.md file:

security_contact_information:
Score (avg): 3.0
[QWEN] The document provides a link to a Security Guide in the documentation and a direct link for reporting vulnerabilities through GitHub. However, it does not provide explicit contact details for security-related inquiries, such as a security email address, PGP public key, security team contact, or general security contact point. Therefore, the information is useful but not fully clear or self-contained for all security-related inquiries.

vulnerability_reporting_process:
Score (avg): 3.0
[QWEN] The document clearly states that vulnerabilities should be reported through the provided GitHub security advisory link: “If you want to report a vulnerability please report it here through github.” This gives a direct reporting channel. However, the process description is very brief and lacks additional helpful details such as what information to include, expected response time, disclosure policy, preferred secure communication method, or guidance on when to use the GitHub form versus another channel.

supported_versions:
Score (avg): 1.0
[QWEN] The document does not specify which versions of the software are currently supported with security updates. There is no mention of supported releases, end-of-life versions, maintenance windows, or a policy explaining how long older versions will receive security fixes.
